newsitem.title: UK: France tops Germany, Japan on corp governance - poll.
newsitem.headline: France tops Germany, Japan on corp governance - poll.

text.p: French firms meet more U.S.-style shareholder demands than those in either Germany or Japan, according to a survey of the world's top five stock markets by U.S. corporate governance consultants Davis Global Advisors.
Among non-English speaking markets, France scored 5.3 on a 10-scale index, compared with Germany's 4.4 and Japan's 3.3. Britain topped the list with a score of 7.6 and the U.S. was second with 7.2.
Davis Global Advisors said its indicators were based on guidelines promoted by British and U.S. institutional investors who now dominate international equity markets.

They measured best practice codes, non-executive directors, split chairman/CEO posts, board committees, voting procedures, voting rights and voting issues, accounting standards, executive pay and takeover barriers.

"Britain outpaced the U.S. thanks to practices that give shareholders more say over strategic corporate decisions, more boards splitting the jobs of chairman and chief executive and the adoption of national corporate governance standards."

France gave more voice to shareholders than the U.S., the report noted. French boards have to get shareholder approval before taking major decisions which could affect stock prices while U.S. coporations don't have to consult, which often sparks shareholder rebellions.

"France also has a higher percentage of large corporations using international or American accounting standards than Germany or Japan, making it easier for international investors to evaluate French financial statements," the report said.

However, French boards "tend to be dominated by powerful chairman/chief executives, leading institutions to question the ability of directors effectively to oversee management. Moreover, companies often feature double-voting shares which dilute the ballot influence of many shareholders".
Like Germany and Japan, France lags well behind the U.S. and Britain in disclosure of executive pay, and proxy voting is tougher, Davis Global Advisors said.
